When an insurer sells an annuity, or a pension plan promises an income for
life, it takes on **longevity risk**: the risk that people live longer than
expected. Every extra year of life is another year of payments. And because
the same trend affects every policyholder at once, this risk does not
diversify away as the portfolio grows.

The single most important assumption behind longevity risk is **mortality
improvement**: how fast death rates will keep falling in the future. In this
post I build a simple but widely used mortality improvement model from
scratch, the **Lee-Carter model**, and use it to answer three practical
questions:

1. How fast has mortality been improving, and at which ages?
2. What improvement does the model project for the future, and how uncertain is it?
3. How much does that matter for the value of an annuity?

## The data

I use England & Wales male mortality data from the
[Human Mortality Database](https://www.mortality.org), which ships with the
R package [StMoMo](https://cran.r-project.org/package=StMoMo) (Stochastic
Mortality Modelling). It contains deaths $D_{x,t}$ and central exposures
$E_{x,t}$ by single age $x$ and calendar year $t$, from 1961 to 2011.

Since longevity risk is mostly about retirement ages, I focus on ages 55 to 100.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(StMoMo)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
blue <- "#06436e"

ages  <- 55:100
years <- 1961:2011

Dxt <- EWMaleData$Dxt[as.character(ages), as.character(years)]
Ext <- EWMaleData$Ext[as.character(ages), as.character(years)]
mxt <- Dxt / Ext   # observed central death rates

# Helper: turn an age x year matrix into a long data frame
to_long <- function(mat, value = "value") {
  as.data.frame(as.table(mat), stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
    setNames(c("age", "year", value)) |>
    mutate(age = as.integer(age), year = as.integer(year))
}
```
:::


The central death rate $m_{x,t} = D_{x,t} / E_{x,t}$ is the number of deaths
per person-year lived. Plotting it on a log scale for a few ages shows the
story at a glance: death rates have fallen steadily at every age, and the
lines are roughly straight, so mortality has fallen at a fairly constant
*percentage* rate each year.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
to_long(mxt, "mx") |>
  filter(age %in% c(65, 75, 85, 95)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, mx, colour = factor(age))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#9ecae1", "#4292c6", "#08519c", "#08306b")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Death rate (log scale)", colour = "Age")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Observed central death rates (log scale), England & Wales males.](index_files/figure-html/fig-rates-1.png){#fig-rates width=768}
:::
:::


## Measuring mortality improvement

Actuaries usually describe these trends as **mortality improvement rates**,
the annual percentage fall in the death rate:

$$
MI_{x,t} = 1 - \frac{m_{x,t}}{m_{x,t-1}} .
$$

An improvement rate of 2% at age 70 means a 70-year-old this year is 2% less
likely to die than a 70-year-old was last year.

Year-to-year rates are noisy, especially at the oldest ages where there are
few deaths, so for the heatmap I use the average annual improvement over the
previous 5 years, $1 - (m_{x,t} / m_{x,t-5})^{1/5}$. Red means mortality
improved, blue means it got worse.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mi_obs <- 1 - mxt[, -1] / mxt[, -ncol(mxt)]   # annual improvement, used later

yrs <- 1966:2011
mi_5y <- 1 - (mxt[, as.character(yrs)] / mxt[, as.character(yrs - 5)])^(1/5)

to_long(mi_5y, "mi") |>
  filter(age <= 95) |>
  mutate(mi = pmax(pmin(mi, 0.05), -0.05)) |>   # cap extremes for readability
  ggplot(aes(year, age, fill = mi)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_abline(intercept = -1919, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       labels = scales::label_percent(), name = "Improvement") +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Age")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Average annual mortality improvement over the previous 5 years, by age and year. The dashed line follows the generation born in 1919.](index_files/figure-html/fig-heatmap-1.png){#fig-heatmap width=768}
:::
:::


Two things stand out:

- **Improvement accelerated** from the 1990s onwards, especially between ages
  60 and 80: the chart gets much redder over time.
- **The pattern runs along diagonals.** A diagonal line in an age-by-year
  chart follows one generation as it ages. Men born after the early 1920s
  (below the dashed line), and particularly those born around 1925–1945, have
  enjoyed much faster improvement than earlier generations. In the UK this is
  known as the **"golden cohort"**. The pale stripe along the dashed line
  itself is the 1919 generation, a well-known quirk of this data linked to the
  irregular pattern of births just after the First World War.

These generational patterns are called **cohort effects**. Keep them in mind;
we will come back to them.

## The Lee-Carter model

Lee and Carter (1992) proposed modelling the log death rate as

$$
\log m_{x,t} = \alpha_x + \beta_x \, \kappa_t + \varepsilon_{x,t},
$$

where

- $\alpha_x$ is the average shape of mortality by age (the "age profile"),
- $\kappa_t$ is a single **period index** that captures the overall level of
  mortality in year $t$; it trends down as mortality improves,
- $\beta_x$ says how strongly each age responds to changes in $\kappa_t$.

The beauty of the model is that it reduces the whole age-by-year surface to
one time series, $\kappa_t$. Forecasting mortality then becomes forecasting
$\kappa_t$.

Rather than the original least-squares fit, I use the Poisson version
(Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt, 2002), which assumes
$D_{x,t} \sim \text{Poisson}(E_{x,t}\, m_{x,t})$. It gives more weight to ages
with more data, which is what we want.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
LC <- lc(link = "log")
LCfit <- fit(LC, data = EWMaleData, ages.fit = ages, years.fit = years,
             verbose = FALSE)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
params <- bind_rows(
  tibble(param = "alpha[x]", x = ages,  value = LCfit$ax),
  tibble(param = "beta[x]",  x = ages,  value = LCfit$bx[, 1]),
  tibble(param = "kappa[t]", x = years, value = LCfit$kt[1, ])
)

ggplot(params, aes(x, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = blue, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~param, scales = "free", labeller = label_parsed) +
  labs(x = "Age / Year", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Fitted Lee-Carter parameters.](index_files/figure-html/fig-params-1.png){#fig-params width=768}
:::
:::


The parameters read naturally:

- $\alpha_x$ rises almost linearly with age: mortality grows roughly
  exponentially with age (Gompertz' law).
- $\beta_x$ is largest at younger retirement ages and falls towards zero at
  100, so younger pensioners have benefited most from the downward trend.
- $\kappa_t$ falls steadily, and more steeply after about 1990, matching the
  acceleration we saw in the heatmap.

## Projecting the future

The standard way to project $\kappa_t$ is a **random walk with drift**:

$$
\kappa_t = \kappa_{t-1} + \delta + \xi_t, \qquad \xi_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2).
$$

The drift $\delta$ is simply the average yearly change in $\kappa_t$. This
has a neat consequence for improvement rates. Ignoring noise, the model's
projected improvement at age $x$ is

$$
MI_x = 1 - \frac{m_{x,t}}{m_{x,t-1}} = 1 - e^{\beta_x \delta},
$$

which is **constant over time** and depends on age only through $\beta_x$.

To capture uncertainty, I simulate 1,000 future paths of $\kappa_t$ over 50
years. Each path gives a full future mortality table.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
h <- 50
set.seed(2026)
LCfor <- forecast(LCfit, h = h)              # central projection
LCsim <- simulate(LCfit, nsim = 1000, h = h) # 1,000 stochastic scenarios
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fan_data <- function(age) {
  a <- as.character(age)
  sims <- LCsim$rates[a, , ]
  tibble(
    age  = paste("Age", age),
    year = as.integer(colnames(LCsim$rates)),
    q05  = apply(sims, 1, quantile, 0.05),
    q25  = apply(sims, 1, quantile, 0.25),
    q50  = LCfor$rates[a, ],
    q75  = apply(sims, 1, quantile, 0.75),
    q95  = apply(sims, 1, quantile, 0.95)
  )
}
fan <- bind_rows(fan_data(65), fan_data(85))
obs <- to_long(mxt, "mx") |>
  filter(age %in% c(65, 85)) |>
  mutate(age = paste("Age", age))

p_fan <- ggplot(fan, aes(year)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), fill = blue, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), fill = blue, alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), colour = blue, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = obs, aes(y = mx), colour = blue, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~age, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Death rate (log scale)")
p_fan
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Death rates at ages 65 and 85: observed (dark), central projection and 50% / 90% intervals.](index_files/figure-html/fig-fan-1.png){#fig-fan width=768}
:::
:::




The fan widens over time: we are fairly confident about next year's mortality,
much less so about mortality in 2050.

### How do projected improvements compare with history?

Let's compare the model's constant projected improvement rates with what was
actually observed over the last 20 years of data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
drift <- mean(diff(LCfit$kt[1, ]))

improvement <- tibble(
  age = ages,
  `Lee-Carter projection (fit 1961–2011)` = 1 - exp(LCfit$bx[, 1] * drift),
  `Observed average 1992–2011` = rowMeans(mi_obs[, as.character(1992:2011)])
) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "source", values_to = "mi")

ggplot(improvement, aes(age, mi, colour = source)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(blue, "#b2182b")) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Annual improvement", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Projected Lee-Carter improvement rates versus observed average improvement, 1992–2011.](index_files/figure-html/fig-improvement-1.png){#fig-improvement width=768}
:::
:::


This is the most important chart in the post. The model projects **less**
improvement than we observed recently, because its drift is an average over
1961–2011, which includes the slower decades of the 1960s and 1970s.

This is a judgement call, not a statistical one: **which history do we
believe is representative of the future?** Let's see how much the answer
depends on it by refitting the model on 1981–2011 only.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
LCfit_recent <- fit(LC, data = EWMaleData, ages.fit = ages,
                    years.fit = 1981:2011, verbose = FALSE)
drift_recent <- mean(diff(LCfit_recent$kt[1, ]))
mi_recent <- 1 - exp(LCfit_recent$bx[, 1] * drift_recent)

tibble(
  Age = c(65, 75, 85, 95),
  `Fit 1961–2011` = (1 - exp(LCfit$bx[, 1] * drift))[as.character(Age)],
  `Fit 1981–2011` = mi_recent[as.character(Age)]
) |>
  mutate(across(-Age, scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1))) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "c")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


| Age | Fit 1961–2011 | Fit 1981–2011 |
|:---:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
| 65  |     2.3%      |     3.1%      |
| 75  |     1.9%      |     2.7%      |
| 85  |     1.2%      |     1.8%      |
| 95  |     0.6%      |     0.7%      |


:::
:::


Same model, same data source, and a noticeably different view of the future,
just from the choice of calibration window.

## From mortality to money: the impact on annuity values

Finally, let's translate this into something an insurer cares about: the
cost of paying a man aged 65 in 2012 an income of 1 per year, at the end of
each year, for as long as he lives.

Following him through time means walking **diagonally** through the
projected table: age 65 in 2012, 66 in 2013, and so on. With
$q = 1 - e^{-m}$ the probability of dying within the year, the annuity
value at interest rate $i$ is

$$
a_{65} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} v^k \, {}_kp_{65}, \qquad
{}_kp_{65} = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \left(1 - q_{65+j,\;2012+j}\right), \qquad v = \frac{1}{1+i}.
$$

For simplicity I stop at age 100 and use $i = 3\%$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cohort_annuity <- function(rates, age0 = 65, year0 = 2012, i = 0.03) {
  n  <- 100 - age0 + 1
  m  <- sapply(0:(n - 1), function(k)
          rates[as.character(age0 + k), as.character(year0 + k)])
  kp <- cumprod(1 - (1 - exp(-m)))
  c(e65 = sum(kp), a65 = sum(kp * (1 + i)^-(1:n)))
}

# 1. No improvement: 2011 death rates frozen forever
frozen <- matrix(mxt[, "2011"], nrow = length(ages), ncol = h,
                 dimnames = list(ages, 2012:(2011 + h)))
no_improvement <- cohort_annuity(frozen)

# 2. Lee-Carter central projection
central <- cohort_annuity(LCfor$rates)

# 3. Distribution across the 1,000 simulated scenarios
sims <- t(sapply(1:1000, function(s) cohort_annuity(LCsim$rates[, , s])))
a_995 <- quantile(sims[, "a65"], 0.995)

tibble(
  Scenario = c("No future improvement", "Lee-Carter central projection",
               "Lee-Carter 99.5th percentile"),
  `Life expectancy at 65 (to age 100)` = c(no_improvement["e65"], central["e65"],
                                          quantile(sims[, "e65"], 0.995)),
  `Annuity value at 3%` = c(no_improvement["a65"], central["a65"], a_995)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, align = "lcc")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Scenario                      | Life expectancy at 65 (to age 100) | Annuity value at 3% |
|:-----------------------------|:----------------------------------:|:-------------------:|
|No future improvement         |               17.92                |        13.09        |
|Lee-Carter central projection |               19.26                |        13.82        |
|Lee-Carter 99.5th percentile  |               20.35                |        14.39        |


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(as.data.frame(sims), aes(a65)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = blue, alpha = 0.7, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = no_improvement["a65"], linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = a_995, colour = "#b2182b", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = no_improvement["a65"], y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.05,
           label = "No improvement") +
  annotate("text", x = a_995, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1.05,
           label = "99.5th percentile", colour = "#b2182b") +
  labs(x = "Annuity value (per 1 of annual income)", y = "Number of scenarios")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Distribution of the annuity value across 1,000 simulated mortality scenarios.](index_files/figure-html/fig-annuity-1.png){#fig-annuity width=768}
:::
:::


The numbers tell the longevity risk story:

- **Ignoring improvement is expensive.** Allowing for projected improvement
  raises the annuity value by about
  5.5%
  compared with frozen 2011 rates. Across a large annuity book, that gap is
  enormous.
- **Uncertainty is material too.** In the 1-in-200 scenario (the 99.5th
  percentile, the same confidence level as Solvency II, though Solvency II
  measures it over a one-year horizon rather than the full run-off used
  here), the annuity is worth a further
  4.2%
  more than the central estimate. That margin is a rough indication of the
  capital needed to withstand longevity risk.

## Limitations and next steps

Lee-Carter is a great starting point, but an actuary should know its blind
spots before relying on it:

- **Calibration window.** As we saw, the projection depends heavily on which
  years we fit. In practice this is where expert judgement comes in.
- **Constant improvement pattern.** Because $\beta_x$ is fixed, the model
  assumes the *age pattern* of improvement never changes. In reality,
  improvement has shifted towards older ages over time.
- **No cohort effects.** The diagonal patterns in the heatmap are invisible to
  Lee-Carter. Models such as Renshaw-Haberman or the Age-Period-Cohort model
  add a cohort term.
- **Understated uncertainty.** The simulations only reflect randomness in
  future $\kappa_t$. They ignore parameter uncertainty (which can be added
  with a bootstrap, e.g. `StMoMo::bootstrap()`) and model uncertainty, so the
  99.5th percentile above is optimistic.
- **The oldest ages.** Data above 90 are thin, and I stopped at age 100. A
  real model would smooth and extrapolate rates to ages 110–120.

In future posts I plan to compare Lee-Carter with the Cairns-Blake-Dowd (CBD)
model, which was designed for pension ages, and to add cohort effects.

## References

- Lee, R. D., & Carter, L. R. (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality.
  *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 87(419), 659–671.
- Brouhns, N., Denuit, M., & Vermunt, J. K. (2002). A Poisson log-bilinear
  regression approach to the construction of projected lifetables.
  *Insurance: Mathematics and Economics*, 31(3), 373–393.
- Villegas, A. M., Kaishev, V. K., & Millossovich, P. (2018). StMoMo: An R
  package for stochastic mortality modeling. *Journal of Statistical Software*,
  84(3), 1–38.
- Human Mortality Database. University of California, Berkeley (USA), and Max
